title: Pan Am 806
summary: Pan Am Flight 806 departed Auckland on 30 January 1974 with 91 passengers and 10 crew for a flight to Los Angeles with stops at Pago Pago and Honolulu. On approach to Pago Pago, the aircraft encountered microburst wind shear. At 23:40:42, the 707 came into contact with trees 3865 ft short of runway 5 threshold while descending through weather. The aircraft impacted the ground 236 feet further and plowed through dense vegetation for another 539 ft before crashing into a three-foot high rock wall. All four engines were torn from the wings and a post-impact fire consumed most of the aircraft, killing 97 persons. Four crew and passengers initially survived but died later.
probable_cause: The flight crew's tardy identification of microburst-induced wind shear. Other factors included poor visibility, lack of altitude and airspeed callouts by the aircrew.

factors.evidence: the flight crew's tardy identification of microburst-induced wind shear
lack of altitude and airspeed callouts by the aircrew
mean rain shower at the airport with reduced visibility on final approach
aircraft came into contact with trees 3865 feet short of runway threshold
aircraft impacted ground and plowed through dense vegetation before hitting rock wall

events.text: Flight 806 descended to 5500 ft and captured the 226 degree radial of the Pago Pago VOR, flying the reciprocal heading of 46 degrees
Approach controller reported mean rain shower at the airport; wind zero three zero (30) degrees at two zero (20), gusting two five (25)
At 23:40:22 co-pilot said you're a little high and at 23:40:33 you're at minimums
First officer stated field in sight then turn to your right followed by hundred and forty knots

At 23:40:42 the 707 came in contact with trees 3865 ft short of the runway 5 threshold; aircraft first impacted the ground 236 feet further and plowed through dense vegetation for another 539 ft before crashing into a three foot high rock wall

notes: NTSB final report detailed and complete
Windshear is now recognized weather phenomenon with detection systems mandated

title: Pan Am 812
summary: Pan Am Flight 812, a Boeing 707, crashed into a mountain near Denpasar, Bali on April 22, 1974 while preparing for approach to Ngurah Rai Airport. Multiple eyewitnesses reported the aircraft was on fire before striking Mesehe Mountain, and the crew appears to have attempted approach from the northwest where terrain was steeper rather than the standard eastern approach.
probable_cause: The aircraft struck a mountain during approach to Denpasar. Investigation concluded the aircraft did not break up in flight, engines were functioning properly, and the aircraft was airworthy. The crew's attempt to approach from the northwest into mountainous terrain was the primary factor.

factors.evidence: Captain Zinke was trying to land from the northwest, where the mountains were located, rather than the usual route from the east
the aircraft descended below the MSL elevation of Mesehe Mountain without terrain clearance
the pilot-in-command requested the visibility by calling but this message was never received by the Bali Tower
it was subsequently found that the aircraft had hit a mountain approximately 37 mi northwest of the Bali airport

events.text: First contact between aircraft and Bali Tower at 15:06 UTC
Flight 812 reported reaching 2,500 feet and requested visibility information
Pilot requested tower visibility information; this message was never received by Bali Tower
Crew descended toward Mesehe Mountain from northwest rather than standard eastern approach
Aircraft struck Mesehe Mountain; tower attempting contact received no response

notes: Investigation hampered by Indonesian Government decision to stop investigation
Multiple eyewitnesses reported fire before impact
Aircraft broke up only on impact, not in flight
Specific cause of crew's navigation decision not documented

title: TWA 514
summary: TWA Flight 514 was diverted to Washington Dulles due to severe weather with high crosswinds on the original approach. During vectoring for a non-precision approach to runway 12, the crew descended to 1800 ft shown on the first checkpoint but became confused about whether they were still on a radar-controlled segment that allowed safe descent. At 11:09:22 a.m. EST, the Boeing 727 impacted the west slope of Mount Weather at 1670 ft above sea level at 230 knots, killing all 92 occupants.
probable_cause: Crew descent below safe altitude due to confusion over instrument approach procedures and lack of clear indication from ATC that they were no longer on a radar vector segment and responsible for their own navigation.

factors.evidence: crew believed they were at a safe altitude when they were actually descended to unsafe altitude

terminology between pilots and controllers differed without either group being aware of the discrepancy; no clear indication had been given by controllers that the flight was no longer on a radar vector segment
cockpit voice recorder indicated confusion in the cockpit over whether they were still under a radar-controlled approach segment
high winds gusting to 49 knots, snow, and reduced visibility were encountered during approach
aircraft impacted west slope of Mount Weather at 1670 ft above sea level

events.text: Flight vectored for a non-precision instrument approach to runway 12 at Dulles, with clearance down to 7000 ft before clearing them for the approach
The jetliner began a descent to 1800 ft, shown on the first checkpoint for the published approach
After reaching 1800 ft there were some 100 to altitude deviations which the flight crew discussed as encountering heavy downdrafts and reduced visibility in snow
At 11:09:22 a.m. EST, the plane impacted the west slope of Mount Weather at 1670 ft above sea level at approximately 230 knot

notes: NTSB investigation found procedural ambiguity resolved by later clarifications
Groundwater proximity warning system was mandated after this accident

title: Martinair 138
summary: A Douglas DC-8 operating a hajj charter flight from Surabaya to Jeddah via Colombo encountered deteriorating weather on approach. The crew descended to 2000 ft and continued descent without sighting the airport, striking the Saptha Kanya mountain range at 4355 ft approximately 40 nautical miles east of Colombo, killing all 191 occupants.
probable_cause: Controlled flight into terrain resulting from descent below safe altitude due to crew misidentification of position relative to airport, relying on onboard Doppler and Weather Radar systems.

factors.evidence: Crew misidentified their position vis-a-vis the airport based on Doppler and Weather Radar systems.
Crew continued descent below minimum altitude without sighting the airport or visual contact.
Colombo area experiencing poor visibility and deteriorating weather on approach.
Aircraft crashed into Saptha Kanya mountain range at 4355 ft approximately 40 nautical miles east of Colombo.

events.text: Aircraft contacted Katunayaka approach at 130 miles out; approach control reported weather and requested crew change to Colombo area control.
Aircraft descended from 35000 ft and was cleared to 2000 ft by approach control, required to report if airport in sight.
Crew did not sight airport and made no further radio contact; aircraft flying at abnormally low level.
Aircraft struck the fifth mountain of Saptha Kanya mountain range at 4355 ft approximately 40 nautical miles east of Colombo with all 191 on board killed.

notes: 182 of 191 occupants were Indonesian Hajj pilgrims
deadliest in Sri Lankan aviation history
